project_scope.selection_mode: Central Texas family-first recognition module with eight project-pool genus doors
project_scope.note: The lesson teaches sedge reproductive structure before the mnemonic. Stem shape is a clue, not a requirement: Cyperaceae culms are often triangular but can be round or flattened.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start at a spikelet, not the stem. In Cyperaceae, each minute flower is subtended by a scale/glume and the superior ovary contains a single ovule, maturing into one hard one-seeded nutlet/achene.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Herbs, often rhizomatous or tufted. Culms are commonly solid and 3-sided; leaves are commonly 3-ranked with closed sheaths, but round culms and other exceptions occur.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers are minute and arranged in spikelets. The perianth is absent or reduced to bristles/scales. Stamens are usually 1–3; styles usually divide into 2–3 branches.
family_diagnostics.fruit: A hard indehiscent one-seeded nutlet/achene, commonly 2- or 3-sided. In Carex the pistillate flower and later the achene are enclosed in a sac-like perigynium.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Use three layers: solid/3-ranked vegetative clues → spikelet with one flower under one scale → one-seeded nutlet. Then switch to the genus-specific structure.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: culm/sheath clue → spikelet → one-seeded nutlet → genus doors → grass/rush comparison
visual_lesson.intro: A sedge is not just a triangular grass. The family becomes much easier when you follow one tiny flower from its scale to the one-seeded nutlet.

steps.title: 1 · Learn the sedge reproductive unit
steps.photo_role: Carex perigynium / scale / achene botanical plate
steps.image_credit: Public domain — Correll & Correll / U.S. EPA, 1972
steps.look_for: A pistillate scale outside a sac-like perigynium, with the achene inside.
steps.why_it_matters: Carex is the largest local sedge door, and the perigynium is a genus-defining structure.

steps.title: 2 · Use the stem and leaf arrangement as a clue
steps.look_for: Often solid culms, commonly triangular in cross-section, and leaves arranged in three ranks with closed sheaths.
steps.why_it_matters: These characters quickly separate many sedges from grasses, but exceptions keep them from being absolute rules.

steps.title: 3 · Carex door: find the perigynium
steps.look_for: Each female flower/achene is enclosed in a bottle-, sac-, or pouch-like perigynium; its shape, veins, hairs, beak and teeth are species-level characters.
steps.why_it_matters: Once you see a perigynium, you are in Carex.

steps.title: 4 · Cyperus door: read the umbrella architecture
steps.photo_role: leaflike involucral bracts + unequal rays + flattened spikelets
steps.look_for: A terminal umbel-like head with several spreading leaflike bracts and spikelets clustered on rays or spikes.
steps.why_it_matters: This whole-inflorescence silhouette gets you to flatsedges quickly.

steps.title: 5 · Eleocharis door: one spikelet at the tip
steps.photo_role: nearly leafless culm + single terminal spikelet + achene tubercle
steps.look_for: Leaf blades absent or reduced to sheaths and exactly one terminal spikelet on each culm; the achene usually retains an enlarged style base/tubercle.
steps.why_it_matters: This is one of the cleanest genus-level patterns in the family.

steps.title: 6 · Rhynchospora and Schoenoplectus doors
steps.photo_role: beaked nutlet / whitetop bracts vs bulrush culm and inflorescence
steps.look_for: Rhynchospora often emphasizes a persistent style base on the nutlet and may have conspicuous white involucral bracts; Schoenoplectus is a bulrush pattern with tall spongy round-to-triangular culms and reduced leaves.
steps.why_it_matters: These two silhouettes are very different even though both are true sedges.

comparisons.title: Cyperaceae vs Poaceae
comparisons.rule: Sedge: commonly solid culm, 3-ranked leaves, closed sheath, one flower under one scale, one-seeded nutlet. Grass: conspicuous nodes, usually 2-ranked leaves, open sheath/collar/ligule, and florets built from lemma + palea inside glumes.

comparisons.title: Cyperaceae vs Juncaceae
comparisons.rule: Sedge flowers are highly reduced in spikelets and usually make one hard one-seeded nutlet. Rush flowers look like tiny ordinary flowers with 6 tepals and mature into a capsule containing several seeds.

comparisons.title: Carex vs Cyperus
comparisons.rule: Carex females have a perigynium around the achene; Cyperus does not and usually announces itself with umbrella-like involucral bracts/rays and flattened spikelets.

visual_lesson.caveat: Do not turn 'sedges have edges' into a rule. Cyperaceae includes round or flattened culms, and Juncaceae can also have flattened stems. Reproductive structure is the safer family confirmation.

family_confusion_cleanup.field_question: If this looks grass-like, which family is it and what single structure breaks the tie?

comparison_matrix.first_lock: Jointed culm with conspicuous nodes; blade-sheath junction has a ligule.
comparison_matrix.confirm: Spikelet has grass floret architecture: glumes outside, lemma + palea around each floret; fruit is a caryopsis.
comparison_matrix.do_not_overtrust: Hollow stems or round stems alone.

comparison_matrix.first_lock: Often solid culm, commonly 3-ranked leaves and closed sheaths; stem may be triangular, round, or flattened.
comparison_matrix.confirm: Minute flower subtended by a single scale; perianth absent/reduced; one hard one-seeded nutlet/achene. Carex adds a perigynium.

comparison_matrix.first_lock: Grass/sedge-like habit but individual flowers still look like tiny conventional flowers.
comparison_matrix.confirm: Six persistent tepals surrounding a superior ovary; fruit is a capsule with several seeds.

decision_key: Can you see conspicuous culm nodes plus a sheath-blade junction with a ligule? → Poaceae door.
No obvious grass node/ligule? Inspect one reproductive unit.
Six tepals around a real flower and later a multi-seeded capsule? → Juncaceae.
Flower reduced beneath a scale and fruit a single nutlet/achene? → Cyperaceae.
exception_locks: Triangular stem supports Cyperaceae but never proves it.
Round stem does not prove Juncaceae.
A grass may have solid internodes; use nodes + ligule + spikelet architecture.
Vegetative plants may remain family-uncertain until the collar/sheath or reproductive unit is visible.
